rationale: Evidence: the baseline (iteration 0 design, which the Evaluator's feedback describes as the current candidate) left the line on every development track. All 60 trials ended off_track with zero finishes. Oval progress was 0.20, s-bend 0.17 and slalom 0.12. max_error was about 0.062 to 0.064 on every track, just past the 0.06 m off-track limit, while rms_error stayed low at 0.02 to 0.03. So the robot tracks the line well on average but is knocked off by occasional large excursions on bends, and the 1.5 to 2 line-loss events per run show it losing the tape at the edge. The failure is recovery at the edge, not average tracking. Speed is the likely driver: at base_speed 1.6 the robot carries too much momentum into bends, and kp 2.5 gives too little corrective turn once it drifts. Changes (controller only, geometry held fixed so the race isolates the controller): (1) kp 2.5 to 3.5, a stronger corrective turn on bends, which is the main lever for max_error; (2) base_speed 1.6 to 1.4, less momentum into bends, so the robot can stay on the tape. This will lengthen completion time, which I accept because surviving to finish is worth 500 points and time is only worth 60 at most; (3) kd 0.2 to 0.4 to damp the extra gain so kp 3.5 does not add jitter. Geometry is unchanged because a wider sensor spread would change the signal gain and confound the test. Expected result: fewer off_track endings, max_error below 0.06 on the oval and s-bend, and line_loss_events near zero. Completion may still be marginal on the slalom. Hypotheses to test next: (a) if max_error is still near 0.06 with kp 3.5, the limit is speed, so drop base_speed further; (b) if steering_oscillation rises sharply, kd is too low for kp 3.5; (c) if the robot is stable but completion_time exceeds 3 s, raise base_speed in small steps (about 0.1) while watching max_error.
